item.title: The Year of Louise of Mecklenburg-Strelitz - Therese of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, Standing alone in the world (Part seven) - History of Royal Women
item.description: Therese wanted to make sure her other children were cared for as well. Therese corresponded constantly with Countess von Lerchenfeld, who had adopted Amalie. The Countess was trying to have Amalie's last name changed to von Lerchenfeld for her future prospects, and this was granted without the right to use the coat of arms.

item.title: Empress Xiaoyuanjing - The Jingtai Emperor's deposed Empress who was greatly loved by her people - History of Royal Women
item.description: Empress Xiaoyuanjing was the first empress to Emperor Daizong (also known as the Jingtai Emperor) of the Ming Dynasty. She was a devoted empress. However, she opposed Emperor Daizong’s proposal to remove the Crown Prince. Because of her opposition, she was deposed and banished to the cold palace. After Emperor Daizong’s death, Empress Xiaoyuanjing was given many privileges and respect from later Ming Dynasty emperors.

item.title: Empress Wang - Emperor Gaozong of the Tang Dynasty's forgotten, childless deposed Empress - History of Royal Women
item.description: Empress Wang of the Tang Dynasty was the first empress to Emperor Gaozong. However, she has largely been forgotten and overshadowed by her successor, Empress Wu Zetian (who later ruled in her own right as the Empress of China).

item.title: Princess Agai - The Yuan Dynasty Princess who tried save her husband from being murdered by her own father - History of Royal Women
item.description: Princess Agai was a princess of the Yuan Dynasty. She was the daughter of Prince Basalawarmi (also known as Bajara Ormi, who was given the title of Prince of Liang). Princess Agai was also the wife of Duan Gong. However, her father feared her husband was becoming too powerful. Tensions would arise between her husband and her father that would lead to tragedy.

item.title: The Year of Louise of Mecklenburg-Strelitz - The life and death of Maria Louise Albertine of Leiningen-Dagsburg-Falkenburg - History of Royal Women
item.description: Maria Louise Albertine of Leiningen-Dagsburg-Falkenburg was born on 16 March 1729 at Heidesheim Castle as the daughter of Count Christian Karl Reinhard of Leiningen-Dagsburg-Falkenburg and Countess Katharina Polyxena of Solms-Rödelheim und Assenheim. She had an elder brother, who died at the age of six and four younger sisters. As such, she was the heiress to the barony of Broich.

item.title: Queen Qianjin - The Queen who was the Sui Dynasty's greatest enemy - History of Royal Women
item.description: Queen Qianjin was the wife of three Turkic Khans. She was made queen in her third marriage to her stepson, Khan Tulan Qaghan.

item.title: Empress Dowager Yang Lihua - The Empress Dowager of Northern Zhou Dynasty who became a Princess of the Sui Dynasty - History of Royal Women
item.description: Empress Dowager Yang Lihua was the last Empress of the Northern Zhou Dynasty. She was the empress consort of Emperor Xuan of the Northern Zhou Dynasty. After Emperor Xuan’s death, Yang Lihua became the Empress Dowager. She was empress dowager for one year because her father, Yang Jian, took the throne and became the first emperor of the Sui Dynasty. Empress Dowager Yang Lihua was cast into the “awkward position of having been empress dowager in one dynasty and being a mere princess in the next.”

item.title: Empress Yuan Qigui - The Empress whose ghost saved an innocent Imperial Consort - History of Royal Women
item.description: Empress Yuan Qigui was the empress consort of Emperor Wen of the Liu-Song Dynasty. Empress Yuan Qigui believed that Emperor Wen treated her fairly. She held a grudge for him that lasted until her death. Empress Yuan Qigui’s ghost was believed to have saved a wrongfully accused imperial consort from death.

item.title: Queen Wilhelmina’s Wedding Gift Tiara - History of Royal Women
item.description: Queen Wilhelmina's wedding gift tiara was part of a parure presented to her on the occasion of her wedding to Prince Henry of Mecklenburg-Schwerin.

item.title: Imperial Consort Zhang - The Imperial Consort who was known for her wise counsel but was ignored by her own husband - History of Royal Women
item.description: Imperial Consort Zhang was an imperial consort to King Fu Jian of the Former Qin Dynasty. However, there is very little information on her.

item.title: The Year of Louise of Mecklenburg-Strelitz - The life and death of the future William I, German Emperor (Part one) - History of Royal Women
item.description: The future William I, German Emperor, was born on 22 March 1797 as the second son of the future King Frederick William III and Louise of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. He had an elder brother, the future King Frederick William IV, and two surviving younger brothers (Charles and Albert) and three surviving younger sisters (Charlotte, Alexandrine and Louise). item.title: The Year of Louise of Mecklenburg-Strelitz - The life and death of the future William I, German Emperor (Part two) - History of Royal Women
item.description: Around 1825, William became romantically involved with his cousin, Princess Elisa Radziwill. However, she was not considered to be sufficiently noble in rank for a marriage with a Prussian prince. His brother's marriage had thus far been childless, and he might even become King one day.

item.title: The Year of Louise of Mecklenburg-Strelitz - The life and death of the future William I, German Emperor (Part three) - History of Royal Women
item.description: On 2 January 1861, King Frederick William IV of Prussia passed away at the age of 65. William and Augusta were now the King and Queen of Prussia. William had his heart set on having a coronation, and this had not been done since 1701

item.title: Empress Zhen - The Empress who committed bigamy - History of Royal Women
item.description: Empress Zhen was the first empress consort of Emperor Cao Pi of the Cao Wei Dynasty. She was the mother of Emperor Ming of the Cao Wei Dynasty. Empress Zhen was originally the wife of Yuan Xi. She committed bigamy when she remarried Cao Pi while she was still married to Yuan Xi. When Zhen became Empress, she would quickly fall out of Emperor Cao Pi’s favour and meet her own tragic end.
